title: Replying to @Yāyo Jones I know we’ll never agree on this, but hopeful...
transcript: Alright, I love to argue with a purist, so here we go. This person says that changing the ending to my Fair Lady is false advertising and compares it to getting your order wrong at a restaurant. The difference between a burger and a chicken sandwich is much greater than the difference between 2018 my Fair Lady and the original. Now, to be fair, the whole point of my video was that the change was significant, so I'm not trying to backpedal here by minimizing it. It's the all or nothing mindset here that I really struggle with, because I would argue there's a lot of space between “this change had a significant impact on my interpretation and takeaway from the piece” vs. “this magically transformed into an entirely different show.” I think a slightly closer analogy would be like they gave you a burger with jalapeños instead of pickles, which, yes, in the culinary world is definitely grounds to send it back. But I still think the metaphor is inapt, because the social convention of a restaurant is reallythat they're trying to cater to you and make sure that you are as pleased as possible. But that really isn't the social contract of theatre. It's not made to order, and satisfaction was never guaranteed. Even in the most safe and traditional revival, you are to a certain extent, handing yourself over to the artists. A restaurant customer might have a deadly allergy to an ingredient that's not on The menu. But I'm pretty sure you're gonna be okay if Eliza leaves Higgins at the end of my fair lady. You're fully entitled not to like it, but it's not false advertising when the material they were reviving was my Fair Lady by any sensible definition. Would you really prefer that Bartlett Sher credit himself as the book writer of this production? Then everyone would complain that he's taking too much credit for work that was done almost entirely by Lerner and Shaw. And if you change the title to “Doolittle: the Untold Story” or whatever, then people are gonna call it false advertising for the completely opposite reason. They're gonna say, I was expecting an adaptation, and all you gave us was my Fair Lady with a different ending tacked on. And that's because a theatre revival is not a jigsaw puzzle that is fundamentally incomplete with one piece out of place. And I would actually argue that it's more of an insult to Lerner and Leowe to imply that all of the rest of the work they did to make this show what it was is rendered somehow meaningless because the director changed one thing.
